_: World practices, with a primary source behind every one.
This exists for the case the measurement cannot cover: a new project, or a
dimension an existing project has no opinion on yet. It is deliberately NOT a
style guide — it is a list of positions someone else already argued in public,
with the link, so a disagreement is with the source rather than with us.
`authority` is the field that decides what happens in a conflict:
standard        a published specification. WCAG is not a preference; a
project that diverges is non-conformant, and saying so is a
statement of fact.
official-docs   the maintainers of the technology say this. Strong, and
still not binding: a team may know their case is different.
convention      widely adopted, sourced, contestable. Defers to any measured
convention in the project.
PRECEDENCE. On an existing project the measured convention wins. A practice
only overrides it when authority is `standard` AND the divergence carries a
cost outside taste — accessibility, security, data loss. Everywhere else the
practice fills a gap and otherwise stays quiet. Walking into a client's
codebase and correcting its style against a blog post is how a consultant gets
ignored on the things that actually matter.
`contested` marks a practice with a real counter-argument. Recording it is the
difference between a catalogue and a sermon.

no-effect-for-server-data.name: Do not fetch server data in an effect
no-effect-for-server-data.what: Server data comes from a caching client (TanStack Query, SWR, RSC, a framework loader) rather than fetch inside a component effect.
no-effect-for-server-data.why: An effect that fetches has no cache, no deduplication, no retry and no request cancellation: two components asking for the same thing ask twice, and a fast remount produces a race whose loser wins.

source.name: React — You Might Not Need an Effect

state-colocation.name: Keep state as close to where it is used as possible
state-colocation.what: State starts local and is lifted only when a second consumer needs it; global stores hold what is genuinely global.
state-colocation.why: State lifted too early re-renders subtrees that do not care and makes every component harder to move.
state-colocation.contested: Teams running a single global store deliberately trade this away for one debuggable state tree; that is a coherent position, not an error.

guard-double-submit.name: Disable submission while a submission is in flight
guard-double-submit.what: A submit control is disabled, or the handler guarded, from the moment submission starts until it settles.
guard-double-submit.why: Without it a double click sends the request twice. On anything that creates a record this produces duplicates that a user cannot undo.

form-library-over-hand-rolled.name: Use a form library once forms have validation
form-library-over-hand-rolled.what: Beyond a single uncontrolled field, forms use an established library rather than hand-rolled state and validation.
form-library-over-hand-rolled.why: Hand-rolled forms re-implement dirty tracking, touched state, async validation and error focus — badly, and differently in each form.

source.name: React — Reacting to Input with State

form-library-over-hand-rolled.contested: A product with two simple forms genuinely does not need the dependency; the practice applies from the point validation appears.

query-by-role.name: Query tests the way a user finds things
query-by-role.what: Tests select by role, label or text before falling back to a test id.
query-by-role.why: A test id asserts the markup. It keeps passing after a change that removes the accessible name, which is exactly the change that breaks the product for someone using a screen reader.

source.name: Testing Library — About Queries, priority order

user-event-over-fire-event.name: Drive interaction with user-event
user-event-over-fire-event.what: Interaction in tests goes through user-event rather than fireEvent.
user-event-over-fire-event.why: fireEvent dispatches one event; a real click is a sequence including focus, pointer and keyboard effects. Tests built on fireEvent pass on components that a user cannot operate.

accessible-name-on-controls.name: Every control has an accessible name
accessible-name-on-controls.what: Icon-only controls carry an accessible name; images carry alt text; form fields are associated with a label.
accessible-name-on-controls.why: A control with no name is announced as 'button' and nothing else. This is a conformance failure, not a preference.

contrast-minimum.name: Text meets the contrast minimum
contrast-minimum.what: Body text reaches 4.5:1 against its background, large text 3:1, in every theme the product ships.
contrast-minimum.why: Below the threshold the text is unreadable for a measurable share of users. The number is defined by the specification, not by us.

keyboard-operable.name: Everything operable by pointer is operable by keyboard
keyboard-operable.what: Interactive behaviour lives on real interactive elements, with the focus and key handling the pattern requires.
keyboard-operable.why: A click handler on a div is unreachable without a mouse. The authoring practices give the expected keys for each pattern, so there is no need to invent them.

logical-properties-for-rtl.name: Use logical properties where direction matters
logical-properties-for-rtl.what: Directional spacing and borders use inline/block properties rather than left/right.
logical-properties-for-rtl.why: A layout built on left/right needs a mirroring layer for right-to-left, and the layer is always incomplete. Logical properties flip with the document.

source.name: MDN — CSS logical properties and values

logical-properties-for-rtl.recommends: 0 where the product ships an RTL language

translation-parity.name: Every message exists in every language
translation-parity.what: Locale files carry the same set of messages; plural categories follow the language's own CLDR rules.
translation-parity.why: A missing key renders as the key. Comparing raw keys across languages is wrong, though: Arabic has six plural categories and English two, so parity is a question about messages, not about keys.

async-has-a-failure-path.name: Every async path has somewhere to fail
async-has-a-failure-path.what: Asynchronous work is guarded, and the failure reaches something that renders: an error state, a boundary, a toast.
async-has-a-failure-path.why: An unhandled rejection leaves the screen in its loading state until reload. The user sees a spinner that never resolves and no reason.

three-screen-states.name: A screen handles loading, error and empty
three-screen-states.what: Every screen that fetches decides what it shows while waiting, when the request fails, and when the result is empty.
three-screen-states.why: The empty state is the first thing a new user sees, and it is the state most often left out. A screen without one looks broken at exactly the moment it should be teaching.

variant-union-over-boolean-flags.name: Express one-of-many as a union, not as boolean flags
variant-union-over-boolean-flags.what: Mutually exclusive appearance or behaviour is one prop with a closed set of values, not several booleans.
variant-union-over-boolean-flags.why: Booleans permit combinations that have no meaning — primary and destructive at once — and nothing rejects them. A union makes the invalid state unrepresentable.

source.name: TypeScript Handbook — Narrowing and discriminated unions

no-invented-props.name: A component's API is its published set of props
no-invented-props.what: Consumers use the props the component declares; new needs change the component rather than being smuggled in through spread or style.
no-invented-props.why: Every escape hatch becomes an undocumented API that the next refactor breaks silently.

source.name: React — Passing props to a component

no-invented-props.contested: A thin wrapper over a DOM element has good reason to forward the rest; the practice is about product components, not primitives.

angular.name: Angular — Accepting data with input properties

design-tokens-format.name: Publish tokens in an interchange format
design-tokens-format.what: Design tokens are exported in the Design Tokens Community Group format alongside whatever the code consumes.
design-tokens-format.why: CSS custom properties are invisible to every design tool. Without an export the system can be copied but not consumed, and the round trip to design never closes.

source.name: Design Tokens Community Group — format specification

code-split-routes.name: Split at the route boundary
code-split-routes.what: Routes load lazily behind a suspense boundary.
code-split-routes.why: Without it the first screen carries the code for every screen, and the cost lands on the visit that decides whether there is a second one.

memoise-on-evidence.name: Memoise from a measurement, not by habit
memoise-on-evidence.what: memo, useMemo and useCallback are added where a profile shows a cost, not applied by default.
memoise-on-evidence.why: Every memo has its own cost and its own dependency array to get wrong. Applied everywhere it slows the app down while looking like optimisation.

source.name: React — useMemo, when to use it

memoise-on-evidence.contested: The React Compiler changes this calculus where it is enabled; the practice is about hand-written memoisation.

one-breakpoint-home.name: Breakpoints have one home
one-breakpoint-home.what: Breakpoint values are defined once and referenced, with the duplication that media queries force being generated rather than typed.
one-breakpoint-home.why: Media queries cannot read custom properties, so the values get repeated by hand and drift apart the first time one changes.

agent-contract-file.name: Machine-readable contract at the repository root
agent-contract-file.what: The working agreement lives in AGENTS.md, the cross-tool file name, with a pointer for tools that expect their own.
agent-contract-file.why: Multiple coding agents now read a repository. A convention documented only in a wiki reaches none of them.
